title: A detector for a silent corruption
subtitle: How the hidden-state extraction backend proves which token it is reading before it writes tens of millions of rows

stats.label: plausible gather conventions, and the engine accepts either
checksum change that proves the engine reads the input
tokens per second over 10.8 million tokens of extraction

lede: The extraction mode of my inference runtime reads a model's internal representation, the input to its language-model head, for every probe, in one forward pass with no generation, at very large batch. The engine's packed-sequence interface takes an input that tells the attention plugin which token's state to gather for each sequence. Two conventions are plausible: the cumulative length, or the cumulative length minus one. The documentation did not settle which this engine expected. A wrong guess still produces well-formed vectors, just the wrong token's, or the next sequence's first token, for every probe. The result would be a silently corrupt dataset of tens of millions of rows. So the backend proves the convention before it extracts anything.
quote: The test runs once per engine load, and it is the difference between a dataset and a disaster.
evidence: TensorRT and TensorRT-LLM engineering: a raw TensorRT hidden-state extraction backend at 25,800 tokens per second over 10.8 million tokens of extraction.
Numerical verification of inference engines: a warm-up detector that tries both of 2 plausible gather conventions and needs a 0.1% checksum change to prove the engine reads its input.
Data provenance for ML pipelines: each hidden state written as a self-describing payload with magic, dtype, shape and hash, appended with a lineage-checked catalog row.
author: Corey James
